content: Hi, a few days ago I started formalizing Linear Temporal Logic in a fork of cslib. Before getting too serious with it I thought I'd check whether anybody's been working on this already :)
I have also been wondering the same thing @Lorenzo Pace. I am using CSLib for my work at Zeroth Research and it seems like we will need LTL in CSLib soon. This came up in our meetings a few times.

Nice. My formalization so far is fairly simple, I provided a semantics on omega-sequences and proven a few lemmata about it. It could be easily extended to transition systems if there was an infinite trace operator, but looking through the library I found only finite trace stuff(?)
At any rate my fork is https://github.com/mell-o-tron/cslib

@Lorenzo Pace If you can create a PR, I’d be happy to review it after I return from my trip on March 12. There’s already a bit of “temporal reasoning” stuff in OmegaSequence/Temporal.lean which should really belong to a theory of LTL. I added that file when I needed some temporal reasoning to prove the closure of omega-regular languages under intersection. It would be nicer if I could appeal to a properly formulated LTL.

One thing about LTL in the context of LTS is that we might want to look into a version of LTL that can talk about not only properties of LTS states, but also properties of LTS labels. While it is always possible to express the latter in terms of the former, such transformations would typically involve ad-hoc history variables that can become unwieldy and ugly.

What do you mean by an “infinite trace operator”? The notion of both finite and infinite executions of LTS are already defined in LTS/Basic.lean and quite a few theorems about them have been proved. (Note however that I plan to refactor that file after I return, so the identifier names may be changed.)

Hi everyone,

Thanks @Ayberk Tosun for mentioning this!

Yes, my colleagues at FBK and I have been working for a while on LTL embeddings in theorem provers. We started with PVS, where we developed a shallow embedding of LTL and used it to certify various model checking algorithms, we have a couple of papers on this:

https://gitlab.fbk.eu/gsindoni/fbk_pdt_cert25
https://gitlab.fbk.eu/gsindoni/Certifying_Rlive_25

We are now porting this shallow embedding from PVS to Lean4, my colleagues @Fajar Haifani and @Christian Micheletti are currently working on this.

We had a look at Lorenzo's formalisation and think that the key difference with our approach is that theirs is a deep embedding (as the HML formalisation). We initially also worked with a deep embedding of LTL, but found that for our purposes, which was proving statements expressed in LTL, a shallow embedding was more appropriate and performed better.

The main difference between the two approaches is that in a shallow embedding, formulas of the logic are directly represented as objects of the theorem prover’s language (e.g. functions from states to booleans), so the prover's automation works on them immediately. In a deep embedding, formulas are instead represented as an explicit inductive syntax tree, with a separate interpretation/satisfaction function defining the semantics. The deep approach is better suited to proving things about the logic itself (e.g. if one wants to prove completeness, cut elimination etc...), while the shallow approach is better suited to proving things in the logic. Both embeddings are useful, for different purposes. 

In any case, we would very much like sync with you all on this and to contribute to CSlib, so we can work together in the same direction!

Tagging also @Alberto Griggio who is also involved in this work.

I agree with the comment by @giulia sindoni above: a shallow embedding is more useful in practice. But it may not be too hard to tweak cslib#413 to become closer to a shallow embedding. Instead of having a type T of "atomic propositions" and a model being of type ωSequence (Set T), we have a type State, an "atomic proposition" being a (wrapped version of) Set State or State → Prop, and a model being of type ωSequence State. The namespace Proposition (which should perhaps be called Formula instead) would allow us to use the dot-notation and write things like φ.and ψ, which is nice.

Another general comment I have is that the LTL in cslib#413 is state-oriented, in the sense that a model is really an infinite sequence of states. But in the context of LTS, a model should be (conceptually) an infinite sequence of alternating states and labels, starting with a state (see the LTS.ωTr in LTS/Basic.lean, which I plan to rename to LTS.OmegaExecution after cslib#325 and cslib#329 are reviewed and merged). In principle, we can always talk about the sequence of labels in terms of the sequence of states by adding history variables. But in practice this can "pollute" the state representation of an LTS and make it unpleasant to work with. For example, you may want to express a notion of fairness by saying that any "action" that is enabled will eventually "fire". Note that an action firing is a property about a state transition, which is not expressible in terms of a state alone. Of course, you can add a history variable to record an action firing. But this is inelegant and you need some logic to implement that history variable. (For instance, the history variable should be "on" for only one state, unless the same action fires in the next step again. The logic soon becomes rather intricate and unpleasant.). So I think we should have at least a version of LTL where there is an atomic proposition that is a Set Label or Label → Prop, which is true in a model if the first step of the model has a label satisfying the proposition.

One more comment: there is a close correspondence between LTL's φ.eventually.always and φ.always.eventually and ∃ᶠ k in atTop and ∀ᶠ k in atTop over ℕ. Some theorems about this correspondence should be provided, so that the LTL theory can leverage the many results about the atTop filter already in mathlib.

Hello,

To give a bit more details about what we already did,
we are also aiming at LTL over theories (at the moment LIA):

Variable : Type := String
State := Variable -> Int --because of LIA
def Trace : Type := Nat → State
def ltl_t_formula : Type := Trace → (Nat → Prop)

@[simp] def lia_atom (atom : LIAAtom) : ltl_t_formula := <ommited>

@[simp] def AND (P Q : ltl_t_formula) : ltl_t_formula := λ trace t => P trace t ∧ Q trace t
@[simp] def OR (P Q : ltl_t_formula) : ltl_t_formula := λ trace t => P trace t ∨ Q trace t
@[simp] def NEG (P : ltl_t_formula) : ltl_t_formula := λ trace t => ¬(P trace t)


@[simp] def Globally (P : ltl_t_formula) : ltl_t_formula := λ trace t => ∀ s : Nat, s ≥ t → P trace s
@[simp] def Finally (P : ltl_t_formula) : ltl_t_formula := λ trace t => ∃ s : Nat, s ≥ t ∧ P trace s
@[simp] def Next (P : ltl_t_formula) : ltl_t_formula := λ trace t => P trace (t + 1)

def models (trace : Trace) (t : Nat) (P : ltl_t_formula) : Prop := P trace t
def valid (P : ltl_t_formula) : Prop := ∀ (trace : Trace), P trace 0
def valid_all (P : ltl_t_formula) : Prop := ∀ (trace : Trace), ∀ (t : Nat), P trace t

the differences:

  • no use of the inductive data type stuff for the formula (shallow)

  • instead of Set T,
    we immediately have def ltl_t_formula : Type := Trace → (Nat → Prop),
    where the Nat is index in the trace (kind of analogous to State → Prop)
    but we use the index (Nat) explicitly .

  • def Trace : Type := Nat → State is basically Cslib.ωSequence State without being inside a structure.
Please use #backticks

Looking at the code that @Fajar Haifani gave above, I'm not sure that there is actually a drastic distinction between "shallow" and "deep" embeddings. Note that even in the "shallow" embedding, there is a ltl_t_formula type of formulas and presumably one will construct expressions of this type in actual applications. It seems to me that whether or not this type is inductive is of little significance when one uses the LTL to do temporal reasoning (as opposed to developing the proof theory of the LTL). Also, as I pointed out in my latest comment in cslib#413, even in the "deep" embedding case, there is no need for the formula type to be an inductive type containing all propositional operators one will ever need. The inductive type can be limited to a small core of operators in terms of which other operators can be defined. This blurs further the distinction between "shallow" and "deep" embeddings.

I have one question about the LTL that @Fajar Haifani gave above: Why does the notion of models has a time argument (t : Nat)? This seems unnecessary for future-time temporal logics. Is the LTL given above part of a temporal logic with past-time temporal operators?

Hi, thanks for your kind interest.

Idk if that was clear earlier, but our use case is automating proof generation. Hence with "performance" we mean "elapsed time" (the time that lean takes to check a file that contains theorems of our interest). More in details, we want to minimise the rewriting steps (the ones performed by simp for example) to translate an LTL formula into a Prop equivalent that we have a proof for.

Please consider the following example:

import Cslib.Logics.LTL.Basic

open Cslib.Logic.LTL
set_option trace.Meta.Tactic.simp.rewrite true

def fairness (ψ : Proposition T) := ψ.eventually.always

def φ_deep : Proposition ℕ := fairness $ Proposition.atom 1

theorem valid_φ_deep (σ : Cslib.ωSequence (Nat → Prop)) : σ ⊧ φ_deep := by
  simp only [φ_deep, fairness, Satisfies]
  sorry

def ShallowLTL (T : Type u) := Cslib.ωSequence (Set T) → Prop

def Fairness (T : Type u) (p : ShallowLTL T)
  := fun σ : Cslib.ωSequence (Set T) => ∀ i : ℕ, ∃ j : ℕ, p ((σ.drop i).drop j)

def Atom (T : Type u) : T → ShallowLTL T
  := fun n σ => n ∈ σ 0

def φ_shallow : ShallowLTL ℕ := Fairness ℕ $ Atom ℕ 1

theorem valid_φ_shallow (σ : Cslib.ωSequence (Set ℕ)) : φ_shallow σ := by
  simp only [φ_shallow, Atom, Fairness]
  sorry

(notice that I implemented it on top of the code in the PR)
In this example, we reduce the goals to the format we know how to tackle.

As you can see, we are bound to define the fairness operator on top of existing constructors in the inductive datatype, with the "deep" embedding. With the shallow embedding instead we can bypass it, as any Cslib.ωSequence (Set T) → Prop is considered a valid LTL formula.

The simplifier then reduces the goals in the two theorems, the "deep" one takes 2 reduction steps more. I think that's easy to see that the problem explodes as the transition systems grow in size (in particular, when the number of definitions grows).

(Ofc in this example one should have also to prove that Fairness and fairness are equivalent, but that's unrelated to the performance topic)

I'm still not sure I understand your concern. You can easily prove a theorem:

theorem fairness_lemma (σ : ωSequence (Set T)) (φ : Proposition T) :
    (σ ⊧ φ.eventually.always) ↔ ∀ i : ℕ, ∃ j : ℕ, (σ.drop (i + j)) ⊧ φ := by
  simp

which will allow you to simplify as if you are using a shallow embedding. Indeed, you can prove a bunch of such lemmas that correspond to the shallow embedding definitions and then rw or simp using them. (By the way, why did you define Fairness directly? Wouldn't you want to define Fairness using Always and Eventually? In that case, you may end up provoing fairness_lemma even if you are using a shallow embedding.)

Furthermore, you may not want to rewrite every temporal operator down to its definition all the time. Sometimes you want to reason at a higher level. For example, you may want to prove that if a model satisfies both φ.eventually.always and φ.implies ψ, then it satisfies ψ.eventually.always. Indeed, the very purpose of having a temporal logic is to be able to do such temporal reasoning. Does a shallow embedding have any advantage over a deep embedding when we do such temporal reasoning?

Hi,

Yes, we also tried this way. We generated such equivalence lemmas when needed, but as we generated more of them we witnessed an explosion in the simplification steps (and therefore running time), because we still have to apply them with the simp or with rw as you pointed out (we tried both). Also, we observed that this approach scaled badly with the transition system size.

The solution we got is to define LTL formulas directly (or "shallowly") as predicates over traces (i.e. Cslib.ωSequence (Set T) → Prop), as you saw in my previous example. This improves the running time of our experiments by a lot, because it lowers the number of simplification steps.

By the way, why did you define Fairness directly? Wouldn't you want to define Fairness using Always and Eventually?

This is just an example to show how we used the shallow encoding to lower the number of simplification steps, compared the deep encoding, and we observed that it scales better with the size of the state space.

Furthermore, you may not want to rewrite every temporal operator down to its definition all the time.

In our experiments instead we do, because we employ a procedure to (try to) close Prop goals on a general basis, but not LTL.

Ofc when proving things manually the inductive datatype approach is more appropriate and does not suffer of this "performance" issue.

To my understanding, the good thing with shallow encoding for performance is that,

In a shallow embedding, the type of a proposition is essentially α → Prop, where α is the type of a "model" of propositions. (For example, for temporal logics, a "model" can be represented by an infinite sequence, as your own examples above show.). You can form the conjunction of two Props. But there is no conjunction of two things of type α → Prop and you'll need to define your own like AND in your first example.

Hi, I just came across this thread and would like to mention another related effort from our side: we have been developing a small Lean library called Lentil:

https://github.com/verse-lab/Lentil/tree/v4.29.0

Lentil is currently a future-only LTL/TLA-style shallow embedding. The core definitions were originally ported from the coq-tla library, although the proofs and the surrounding infrastructure are written in Lean. At the semantic level, executions are represented essentially as Nat -> σ, where σ is the state type, and formulas are predicates over such executions. So this should be fairly close to ωSequence σ, although we have not yet tried to align the library with CSLib's ωSequence interface.

In contrast to the automation-oriented use case discussed above, our current development is more oriented toward manual proofs and object-level temporal reasoning, rather than automated proof generation or rewriting everything down to first-order/SMT-style goals. For that reason, we also built a lightweight proof mode for LTL-style reasoning. Partly this was just fun to experiment with, but the more serious motivation was that, while Iris proof mode (IPM) is a great source of inspiration, it felt rather heavyweight for the much simpler setting of future-only LTL. (That said, we are not ruling out moving to an IPM-based implementation in the future if that turns out to be useful.)

One limitation is that Lentil is not currently designed around LTSs, and we have not yet considered how to express labels/actions from a CSLib LTS interface. So at the moment it is mostly state-trace oriented.

We have used the proof mode to mechanize the LTL rules from this paper. The mechanization is still in a private repo so I cannot point to it yet, but I could share a screenshot showing what the proof script and proof state look like if that would be useful.

Hope this could be a data point for the discussion!

Qiyuan Zhao said:

At the semantic level, executions are represented essentially as Nat -> σ, where σ is the state type, and formulas are predicates over such executions. So this should be fairly close to ωSequence σ, although we have not yet tried to align the library with CSLib's ωSequence interface.

Cslib's ωSequence σ is just a one-field structure wrapping a function of type Nat -> σ. There is enough infrastructure so that you can use an s : ωSequence σ pretty much like s : Nat -> σ, including function application expressions like s 0. The only thing in practice that exposes the difference is that you can't define an ωSequence σ by recursing on its Nat index, which you can easily work around by having a helper function of type Nat -> σ (which can be defined recursively) and then coerce it to ωSequence σ.

One limitation is that Lentil is not currently designed around LTSs, and we have not yet considered how to express labels/actions from a CSLib LTS interface. So at the moment it is mostly state-trace oriented.

I think it is very easy to handle the labels in the temporal logic, as follows:
(1) The model of a temporal logic formula contains not just a state sequence ss : ωSequence State, but also a label sequence xs : ωSequence Label. The idea is that (ss, xs) represent the infinite execution (ss 0), (xs 0), (ss 1), (xs 1), (ss 2), (xs 2), ...
(2) In addition to state predicates, we add also "label predicates". Then we define a label predicate to be true in a model (ss, xs) iff the label predicate is true in xs 0.
That's it.
